content.text: Searching for foundational literature on cross-validation and prediction error estimation. The goal is to identify seminal surveys and key papers that establish the theoretical basis for in-sample versus out-of-sample evaluation methods. Two relevant papers include a survey by Arlot and Celisse (2010) on cross-validation and a paper by Efron (1983) on error rate estimation improvement.

content.text: Initial focus is on understanding the concept of "optimism" in error estimation, as defined by Efron (2004). The apparent error, or resubstitution error, is explicitly defined as the difference between expected test error and expected training error. Examining how fitting to data reduces training error by capturing sample-specific noise is also important. Considering Efron (1983) "Estimating the Error Rate of a Prediction Rule: Improvement on Cross-Validation" for related insights.

content.text: Initial search query will focus on 'statistical learning evaluation correction estimation generalization'. This aims to identify relevant survey papers. The goal is to avoid forcing results, prioritizing strict relevance to the core concepts. The initial query will be refined if this does not yield sufficient results.

The search focuses on literature that contextualizes how a constant residual translates into an additive correction within a statistical learning framework, specifically targeting surveys and foundational works. This is to support an explanation of the specific prediction error in the provided example, avoiding any suggestion of new research, novel algorithms, or performance claims. The search will be limited to publications before November 2026, prioritizing high-impact venues or highly-cited papers.

Initial focus is on survey papers and foundational works addressing generalization error and correction methods in statistical learning. Arlot & Celisse (2010), Efron (2004, 1983), and Stone (1974) appear highly relevant to cross-validation and optimism correction, suggesting these should be prioritized. Further selections will aim to complement these with papers explaining the concept of constant residuals within the context of statistical learning.

Focusing on predictive evaluation and generalization, Geisser (1975) introduces cross-validation to separate observation estimation from prediction. Cawley & Talbot (2010) reveals that tuning or correcting on the same observations leads to selection bias, while Mallows (1973) penalizes in-sample fit to address bias. Akaike (1974) and Kohavi (1995) further highlight that in-sample evaluation is overly optimistic, emphasizing the need for explicit penalties and out-of-sample validation. Raschka (2018) provides a broader survey of model evaluation best practices.

Freedman (1983) offers a core demonstration of why model selection based on sample residuals results in biased performance estimates. Breiman (2001) provides a contrasting perspective on how to evaluate models by separating goodness-of-fit from predictive generalization. These works solidify the need to address the overoptimistic bias arising from in-sample evaluation and model correction.
